segments.say: Every plan to change something eventually meets a bad day. You skip the walk. You eat the thing you said you wouldn't. You stay up too late, again. And what happens next, in the hours after a slip, matters more than the slip itself.

But first, a question. Why do some days feel like a better time to begin than others? A Monday. The first of the month. New Year's Day. Your birthday. Nothing about the world really changes at midnight. And yet something in us does.

In 2014, Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis looked at several kinds of data. Internet searches for the word diet. Daily visits to a university gym. And commitments people made online to reach a personal goal.

show.who: Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman & Jason Riis
show.what: Found that searches for 'diet' and visits to a university gym rose at the start of weeks, months and years, and after birthdays

segments.say: All of them rose at the beginnings of things. The start of a week. The start of a month. The start of a new year. And, at the gym, just after a person's birthday. The researchers called it the fresh start effect.

Their explanation was gentle. Those landmarks seem to draw a line between an old self and a new one. The mistakes feel like they belong to the person you were last week. On the new page, you feel a little more like someone who could do it.

A year later, the same team tested whether you could create that feeling with words alone. They described the very same day in different ways. For some people, a date in March was simply the third Thursday of the month. For others, it was the first day of spring.

show.who: Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman & Jason Riis
show.what: Found that describing a date as the start of a new period made people more eager to begin a goal on it

segments.say: When the day was framed as a beginning, the first day of spring, people were more eager to start a goal on it. Nothing about the day had changed, only the way it was described. A fresh start, it seems, is partly something we tell ourselves.
And the good news is, you don't have to wait for January. Any meaningful marker can work. A new season. The first day after a trip. Even the start of tomorrow, if you decide to see it that way.

show.sub: You can make your own landmarks

segments.say: But there's a darker pattern, too, and almost everyone knows it. You break a rule a little, and then, because it's already broken, you break it a lot. Researchers gave this a wonderfully blunt name.

show.sub: When a slip becomes a fall

segments.say: In 1975, C. Peter Herman and Deborah Mack ran what was described as a taste test. Some volunteers first drank a milkshake. Others didn't. Then everyone was given tubs of ice cream to taste and rate, and could eat as much as they liked.

show.what: Found that dieters who had already drunk a milkshake went on to eat more ice cream, not less

segments.say: People who weren't dieting ate less ice cream after the milkshake, which makes sense. They were fuller. But people who were trying hard to restrict their eating often ate more ice cream after the milkshake. The diet was already broken for the day, so why hold back now? Janet Polivy and Peter Herman later wrote about this pattern, and it became known as the what-the-hell effect.

It seems to come from all-or-nothing thinking. A rule is either kept perfectly, or it's broken. There's no middle. And once it's broken, the rule stops protecting you. It's not just about food. You may know the same feeling with sleep, or screens, or studying.

Researchers who study relapse saw the same thing. The psychologists Alan Marlatt and Judith Gordon described what they called the abstinence violation effect. After a first slip, people often see themselves as having failed completely, and that very feeling of failure makes the next slip more likely. It isn't the slip that does the damage. It's the story told about it.

The way out is the same kindness we met earlier tonight, in the study about self-forgiveness and procrastination. One slip is just one slip. It's information, not a verdict. The very next choice is still free, and it still counts.
There's one more thing that helps people start again, and it's the least exciting idea of the night. Rest. We often treat tiredness as a lack of motivation. But very often, it's simply tiredness.

In 1993, K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. They found that the best students practised a great deal, in focused sessions, often in the morning. And they also reported sleeping more, including more afternoon naps, than the less accomplished students.

show.who: K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe & Clemens Tesch-Römer
show.what: Studied violin students in Berlin and found the best ones practised in focused sessions, and also slept and napped more

segments.say: That study is famous for its message about practice, which later research has debated a lot. But the quieter detail is often forgotten. The people who worked hardest also rested the most. Effort and rest aren't opposites. They're two halves of the same rhythm.
So let's go back to where we started tonight. The alarm goes off. Some mornings you get up with ease. Some mornings you can barely move. Now, perhaps, that difference makes a little more sense.

show.cap: The alarm clock, one more time

segments.say: On the easy mornings, many things are lined up. You're rested. Something today feels like it matters. You can picture the first small step. And maybe a habit carries you to the kettle before you've even thought about it.

Let's walk back through the night. We started with the body's drives, and with curiosity, the urge to explore for its own sake. We met dopamine, and the difference between wanting something and liking it. We saw how rewards can strengthen a behaviour, and also how they can quietly drain the fun out of something you already loved.

show.title: Tonight, we explored
items: Rewards that help and rewards that harm

segments.say: We saw that people need to feel some choice, some skill, and some connection. That a clear goal helps, but so does picturing the obstacle. That small steps of progress are powerful fuel. And that unfinished things tend to tug at us.

We looked at self-control, and how some famous findings shrank when they were tested again. We looked at procrastination, as a way of escaping a bad feeling, and at the strange distance between ourselves and our future selves. We saw how belief in yourself can help, a little, and how other people lift us, slow us, and quietly guide us.
And we ended with habits that carry us without asking, with flow, when the work becomes its own reward, with meaning, and with the gentle science of starting again.

If there's one idea to take with you, it might be this. Motivation is not a fixed amount that some people have and others lack. It rises and falls with sleep, with setting, with people, with meaning, and with how kind you are to yourself after a bad day. And much of that can be gently changed.

show.sub: Motivation is not a fixed amount

segments.say: And for now, there's nothing more to change, and nothing more to do. So let's slow everything right down, and let the night take over.
